1) Ciliary-body (uveal) melanoma with extrascleral extension presenting as a pigmented episcleral mass — Most likely. Ultrasound biomicroscopy shows a dome-shaped ciliary body tumor and a ciliary artery channel connecting intrascleral and extrascleral tumor portions, which is classic for a primary ciliary-body melanoma with transscleral extension.

2) Ciliary-body melanocytoma (benign pigmented tumor) with extrascleral extension — Less likely. Melanocytoma can be very pigmented and locally invasive but is much less common in the ciliary body and typically has more benign behavior; vascular channel and dome-shaped mass favor melanoma.

3) Primary conjunctival melanoma (epibulbar) invading inward into sclera/ciliary body — Possible but less likely given UBM evidence of a primary intraocular (ciliary) mass projecting outward rather than a conjunctival primary invading inward.

4) Invasive primary acquired melanosis (PAM) of the conjunctiva with progression to melanoma and scleral/ciliary invasion — Uncommon but in the differential when there is an episcleral pigmented lesion; clinical history and surface features would help distinguish.

5) Metastatic pigmented tumor to the ciliary body/episclera (eg, metastatic cutaneous melanoma) — Possible but less likely without known primary and because UBM supports a primary intraocular origin.

Key implications and recommended next steps (for the treating team)
- Urgent ocular oncology referral.
- Cross-sectional orbital imaging with contrast (MRI with orbital protocol) to define scleral breach and extent of extrascleral extension.
- Comprehensive ocular exam including dilated fundus exam and gonioscopy; anterior-segment photography for baseline.
- Systemic metastatic workup if melanoma confirmed (liver imaging ± CT chest/abdomen, liver function tests).
- Discuss definitive management options (local resection +/- plaque radiotherapy, enucleation) and need for histopathologic diagnosis when indicated.

These ranked diagnoses are based on the provided UBM findings and a well-circumscribed pigmented episcleral lesion with a connecting vascular channel.
